newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Chronology of events in war-ravaged Angola.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of events in war-ravaged Angola.

text.p: The Angolan government and its former UNITA rebel foes have made enough progress implementing a two-year-old peace treaty to satisfy the United Nations that its peacekeeping mission can start to withdraw.
Following is a chronology of key events:

1975 - Left-wing revolution in Portugal spells end of Lisbon's 500-year-old African empire. In colony of Angola, three main guerrilla groups -- Jonas Savimbi's National Union for the Total Independence of Angola (UNITA), the Marxist Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola (MPLA) and the National Liberation Front of Angola (FNLA) -- share power.
Aug 29: Their transitional government collapses.
Nov 11: Independence Day. Portuguese forces withdraw. MPLA backed by Cuban troops holds capital. South Africa backs UNITA.
1976 - MPLA crushes FNLA and drives back UNITA.
1979 - MPLA leader Agostinho Neto dies, replaced by Soviet-trained Jose Eduardo dos Santos.
1987 - South African force enters southeast Angola to thwart MPLA and Cuban offensive against UNITA.
1988 - South Africans withdraw after U.S. mediation. Angola, South Africa, Cuba sign deal linking Namibian independence from South Africa with exit of 50,000 Cuban troops by mid-1991.
1989 - At African summit in Zaire, dos Santos and Savimbi agree on ceasefire, which collapses in August.
Oct 26: MPLA Central Committee approves multi-party democracy after 15 years of one-party rule.
April 28: MPLA ditches Marxism-Leninism for social democracy to prepare for general elections.
May 1: MPLA and UNITA initial peace pact in Portugal providing for ceasefire and elections by November 1992.
May 31: Dos Santos, Savimbi sign peace accord in Lisbon.
Sept 29-30: Angolans vote in first multi-party election for president and 223-seat national assembly.
Oct 6: UNITA withdraws from the newly unified armed forces accusing government of election fraud.

Oct 17: MPLA wins 53.7 percent and UNITA 34.1 percent of national assembly vote. Dos Santos takes 49.57 percent and Savimbi 40.07 percent of presidential vote, forcing second round. U.N. certifies polls generally free and fair.
Oct-Nov: Fighting flares, more than 300 people killed in Luanda as UNITA refuses to accept election results.
January: MPLA offensive against UNITA in major cities with heavy casualties. Fighting continues through year.
November: U.N.-arranged peace talks open in Lusaka, Zambia.
Aug 29: Southern African Development Community says government and UNITA agree on U.N. peacekeeping force. Fighting continues through to October.
Oct 18: U.N. mediator Alioune Blondin Beye announces agreement in principle between government and UNITA to end war.
Nov 20: Angolan government and UNITA sign peace accord.
Jan 26: UNITA and government negotiators convene joint commission overseeing implementation of peace accord, swap accusations of ceasefire violations.
Feb 22: UNITA and government say their forces demobilising, but pace is slow. Clashes continue in central Angola.
May 6: Dos Santos and Savimbi hold peace summit in Lusaka, reiterate commitment to peace accord.
Sept 5 - Brazilian troops are among first peacekeepers.
March 1: Savimbi and Dos Santos agree to form unity government and merge forces in national army by July.
July 1 - Government begins disarming civilians.
Aug 20 - Extraordinary UNITA congress rejects nomination of Savimbi for vice-president in unity government.
Sept 9 - Five UNITA generals arrive in Luanda for integration into Angolan Armed Forces.
Sept 24 - Demobilisation of underage soldiers begins.
Nov 13 - MPLA-dominated parliament passes constitutional amendments to extend its mandate for a minimum two years.
Nov 21 - U.N. announces wind-down of 6,500-man peacekeeping operation in Angola, starting in December.
